claims.text: A high concentration of lightweight elements produces severe atomic-level lattice distortion.
Severe lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion and thereby increases mechanical strength.
Incorporating passivating elements such as Cr or Al promotes formation of a continuous, adherent oxide layer.
A continuous, adherent oxide layer protects the alloy against corrosion and high-temperature oxidation.
The baseline lightweight HEA has moderate strength because its passivating-element concentration and lattice distortion are not optimized.
The baseline lightweight HEA has incomplete corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Cr or Al content can be increased while preserving the lightweight nature of the alloy.
Controlled melting, casting, and homogenization will ensure uniform element distribution and controlled microstructural evolution.
Passivating elements react during high-temperature exposure to form a compact protective oxide scale.
The compact oxide scale minimizes further oxidation and reduces corrosion attack.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will have increased yield strength.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will exhibit a lower oxidation weight-gain or oxide-scale-growth rate at 600–800 °C.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will exhibit a reduced corrosion rate in saline environments.
The protective oxide scale is expected to remain stable up to approximately 800 °C.
Above approximately 900 °C, oxide-scale destabilization may cause the hypothesized protection to fail.
Cyclic or dynamic loading may promote cracks in the protective layer and cause the hypothesized protection to fail.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in mechanical strength and oxidation/corrosion resistance relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe a continuous protective oxide and increased lattice distortion correlated with performance would falsify the hypothesis.
